reveals.label: Cell 1: Alleles vs Observable trait
reveals.question: 1. Distinguish between the terms 'genotype' and 'phenotype' using Ben's Huntington's diagnosis.
reveals.expectedAnswer: Genotype = allele pair (Hh); Phenotype = observable condition (Huntington's disease chorea/neurodegeneration)
reveals.answer: Genotype = allele pair (Hh); Phenotype = observable condition (Huntington's disease chorea/neurodegeneration)

reveals.label: Cell 2: Pedigree symbols
reveals.question: 2. In a standard clinical pedigree chart, what do a square, a circle, and a shaded symbol represent?
reveals.expectedAnswer: Square = male; Circle = female; Shaded = clinically affected individual
reveals.answer: Square = male; Circle = female; Shaded = clinically affected individual

reveals.label: Cell 3: Independent events
reveals.question: 3. If Ben (Hh) and his unaffected wife (hh) already have two children, what is the probability their third child inherits H?
reveals.expectedAnswer: Still 50% (1 in 2) — every conception is an independent genetic event
reveals.answer: Still 50% (1 in 2) — every conception is an independent genetic event

reveals.label: Cell 4: Chromosome 4
reveals.question: 4. Why does an autosomal disorder affect biological sons and daughters equally?
reveals.expectedAnswer: The HTT gene lies on an autosome (chromosome 4), not on the X or Y sex chromosomes
reveals.answer: The HTT gene lies on an autosome (chromosome 4), not on the X or Y sex chromosomes

reveals.label: Cell 5: Earlier & more severe
reveals.question: 5. Define 'genetic anticipation' in trinucleotide repeat disorders.
reveals.expectedAnswer: Symptoms appearing at an earlier age and with greater severity in successive generations due to CAG repeat expansion
reveals.answer: Symptoms appearing at an earlier age and with greater severity in successive generations due to CAG repeat expansion

reveals.label: Cell 6: Synoptic TA 2.2 link
reveals.question: 6. Why does OCR require a Topic Area 2.2 mutation diagram alongside Ben's pedigree for P11?
reveals.expectedAnswer: To link the molecular cause (expanded CAG triplet repeat in HTT exon 1) directly to the inheritance pattern
reveals.answer: To link the molecular cause (expanded CAG triplet repeat in HTT exon 1) directly to the inheritance pattern

courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology · Unit F172: Genetics (Topic Area 3 / NEA Task 2)
ocrSpec: Topic Area 3.1.1 (Risk assessment & family trees) + Synoptic Topic Area 2.2 (Mutation & inheritance diagrams)
focus: Constructing Standard Clinical Pedigree Charts, Punnett Squares & Mutation Schematics for Ben's Family (P11), Interpreting Patient Meaning (M6), and Discussing Whole-Family Inheritance & Anticipation Dynamics (D4)
deliverable: 75-minute classroom deck & diagram construction workshop enabling learners to draw clinical pedigree, Punnett square, and CAG-expansion diagrams for Ben's case study (P11), explain what they mean for Ben (M6), and discuss inheritance patterns, non-skipping generations, independent probability, and paternal anticipation across the family (D4).

objectives.knowledge: Construct accurate clinical diagrammatic representations (3-generation pedigree chart, autosomal dominant Punnett square, and HTT CAG mutation schematic) for Ben's case study context (P11).
objectives.application: Explain clearly what the pedigree, Punnett square, and repeat-expansion diagrams mean directly for Ben as the patient (M6).
objectives.evaluation: Discuss what the diagrammatic representations reveal about autosomal dominant inheritance, adoption-masked vertical transmission, independent pregnancy probabilities, and paternal genetic anticipation across Ben's family (D4).

terminology.def: The first affected family member bringing a genetic disorder to clinical attention (Ben), marked with an upward-right arrow on a standard clinical pedigree chart.

Standardised Genomics Education Programme symbols: square = male, circle = female, diamond = unspecified sex/unborn fetus, shaded = affected, open = unaffected, square brackets = adoption, Roman numerals = generations (I, II, III).
A genotype carrying one expanded dominant HTT allele (H) and one normal recessive allele (h); a single dominant copy causes disease with equal risk to male and female offspring.
Each conception is an independent meiotic event with a fixed 50% (1 in 2) probability of transmitting H, regardless of whether older siblings inherited H or h.

Progressive expansion of unstable CAG repeats across generations causing earlier onset and greater severity — markedly more frequent during spermatogenesis (paternal transmission) due to continuous cell divisions and replication slippage.

theoryPoints: Standard Clinical Pedigree Rules (Genomics Education Programme — P11): Squares = males, circles = females, diamond = unborn child of unknown sex; shaded = affected (Ben, II-1), open = unaffected (wife, II-2), '?' = unknown biological parents (I-1, I-2) with adoption brackets [ ] around Ben; Roman numerals I–III for generations, Arabic numbers left-to-right, arrow pointing to proband Ben.

Autosomal Dominant Punnett Square & Topic Area 2.2 Mutation Diagram (P11): Cross Ben (Hh) × Unaffected Wife (hh) → gametes H, h × h, h → 50% Hh (affected) : 50% hh (unaffected), ratio 1:1. Synoptically include exon 1 HTT CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion schematic (≤26 normal vs ≥40 pathogenic polyQ misfolding).

Direct Meaning for Ben as the Patient (M6 — Patient Focus): Ben is heterozygous (Hh) with ≥40 CAG repeats (100% full lifetime penetrance); he must have inherited the expanded allele from at least one biological parent (or rarely a new intermediate-allele expansion); his progressive neurodegeneration is certain, and every gamete he produces carries a 50% chance of transmitting H.

Whole-Family Inheritance Discussion (D4 — Case Study Context): Autosomal dominant conditions normally appear in every generation and do NOT skip generations — Ben's missing family history is strictly an artefact of adoption, NOT recessive skipping. Equal transmission to sons and daughters (autosomal, chr 4). Each of his 3 children (6yo daughter, 3yo son, unborn baby) carries an independent 50% risk. Crucially, paternal transmission during spermatogenesis elevates meiotic DNA slippage risk (genetic anticipation), risking earlier or juvenile onset in his offspring.

workedExample.title: Building All 3 P11 Diagrams + Scaling to M6 & D4
workedExample.subtitle: Exact clinical conventions required for full Pass, Merit, and Distinction marks

steps.label: Diagram 1 — 3-Generation Pedigree (P11)
steps.detail: Gen I: Biological parents (square I-1, circle I-2 marked '?' unknown status) connected by dashed/bracketed adoption line to Gen II: Ben (shaded square II-1, proband arrow, genotype Hh) married to unaffected wife (open circle II-2, genotype hh). Gen III: 6yo daughter (open circle III-1, '50% at-risk'), 3yo son (open square III-2, '50% at-risk'), unborn fetus (open diamond III-3 with 'P', '50% at-risk').

steps.label: Diagram 2 — Punnett Square + Mutation Schematic (P11)
steps.detail: Labelled 2×2 Punnett square (Ben Hh × Wife hh → 2 Hh : 2 hh = 50% affected, 50% unaffected) paired with a Topic Area 2.2 chromosome 4p16.3 HTT exon 1 diagram showing normal (≤26 CAG) vs expanded (≥40 CAG) trinucleotide repeat insertion.

steps.label: Meaning for Ben (M6) vs Family Discussion (D4)
steps.detail: M6 interprets Ben's own status (Hh, 100% penetrant, 50% transmission per sperm). D4 evaluates family-wide implications: no true generation-skipping (masked by adoption), debunking the Gambler's Fallacy across all 3 children, sex-independent autosomal risk, and paternal CAG expansion causing genetic anticipation.

hingeQuestions.question: On Ben's clinical pedigree chart, how should his unborn third child (sex not yet known) and his unknown biological parents be represented?
options: Unborn child as a shaded circle; biological parents omitted completely
Unborn child as a diamond (with 'P' / pregnancy indicator) and biological parents in Generation I marked with '?' linked to Ben with adoption brackets [ ]
Unborn child as a crossed-out square; biological parents as unaffected shaded squares
Unborn child as a triangle; biological parents as homozygous recessive hh
hingeQuestions.explanation: Standard clinical pedigree nomenclature (NHS Genomics Education Programme) uses a diamond for unspecified sex/pregnancy, '?' for unknown clinical status, and square brackets [ ] to denote adoption.

hingeQuestions.question: Why does Huntington's disease appear to have 'skipped a generation' in Ben's family, and how should this be explained for Distinction D4?
options: Huntington's disease is autosomal recessive, so unaffected carriers hid the allele

Autosomal dominant full-penetrance HD does NOT skip generations — the apparent absence of family history is masked by Ben's adoption at age 2 (or rarely expansion from a parental intermediate allele of 27–35 repeats)
Because HD is X-linked and cannot pass from father to son
Because Ben's symptoms were caused purely by environmental stress
hingeQuestions.explanation: True full-penetrance autosomal dominant traits do not skip generations; explaining how Ben's adoption masks vertical transmission (alongside intermediate allele expansion and paternal anticipation) demonstrates Distinction-level D4 mastery.

plenary: P11 requires accurate, clinically labelled diagrams: a 3-generation pedigree (with adoption & pregnancy symbols), an Hh × hh Punnett square, and an HTT exon 1 CAG mutation diagram.
M6 translates these diagrams directly for Ben (heterozygous Hh, 100% penetrance ≥40 repeats, 50% transmission probability).
D4 critically discusses family-wide inheritance: non-skipping autosomal dominance masked by adoption, independent 50% risk per child, and heightened paternal anticipation risk during spermatogenesis.
